extracted.subtask_description: Practical classroom methods and evaluative standards for elementary-school instruction (penmanship, recitation, arithmetic drills, class exercises, classroom management) including how to structure lessons, assess pupil work, and organize pupil committees. Emphasis is on concrete exercises, sequential mastery, and mild moral/behavioral management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concrete object-lessons and guided questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a concrete object and use directed questions to lead pupils to observe, hypothesize, and reason (example: the teacher shows a chestnut burr and asks 'Do you know what this is?' and 'Do you know what it is for?'), encouraging all to 'listen attentively.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model: show object, ask successive questions about form/function, allow pupils to propose reasons, correct misconceptions gently, and conclude with an explanation tying observations to broader principles (e.g., protection of developing fruit). Encourages active observation, oral participation, and inductive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Series of writing lessons (sequential progression)
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange the steps of penmanship into a posted series of lessons (beginning with straight lines, then elementary parts of letters, then letters themselves) and require each pupil to practice each lesson until they 'could write it well' before passing to the next.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation details: prepare a large posted sheet with lessons; have writing-books of three sheets folded and ruled by pupils; require practice until teacher marks 'Passed' or 'P.' under the line. Allow individuals to progress independently so the advanced are not retarded by others. Apply the same principle to other studies to add variety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit passing criteria and page standards for penmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond correct formation of letters, additional requisites must be met before a pupil may 'pass' a lesson: the page must not be soiled or blotted, no paper wasted, no leaf torn out; sometimes one line suffices but often a full page is expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher inspects writing books at set times. Usually one well-formed line can permit passing, though commonly a page or sheet would be practiced before a pass. Use brief pencil remarks to call attention to faults when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of arbitrary correction marks (symbolic faults list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt a simple set of correction marks, each indicating a particular fault in penmanship, often with some connection between the sign and the fault (e.g., lengthening letters in red ink to show too short). The principal criticisms are listed as: 'Strokes rough. Curve wrong. Bad termination. Too slanting, and the reverse. Too broad, and the reverse. Not parallel. Form of the letter bad. Large stroke made too fine, and the reverse. Too tall, or too short. Stems not straight. Careless work. Paper wasted. Almost well enough to pass. Bring your book to the teacher. Former fault not corrected.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a catalogue of these marks with explanations and post it where accessible so marking is rapid, consistent, and training is systematic. Use the marks for quick, memorable feedback; sometimes more detailed oral instruction is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind committee examination of writing books by older pupils
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrust the examination of writing-books to a Committee of older/advanced pupils who decide upon books without knowing the writers' names (each page has the name corner turned down). The Committee has plenary powers; their decisions are final though they may be impeached if improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: unbiased judgment, peer responsibility, scalability. Ensure anonymity (turned-down corner), clear duties, and consequences for misuse of authority. This delegated examination works for months with little diminution of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding monotony by varying exercises and applying the 'series' principle broadly
rubrics_metrics.description: The same principle of arranging steps into a series and requiring pupils to pass regularly may be applied to other studies; variety in exercise types prevents weariness of monotonous drill (writing often becomes tedious without plans for interest/variety).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotate exercise types, introduce novel but structured activities (e.g., Topic Exercise, Shopping Exercise, Singing), and periodically change measures like committees so they do not become mere form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral, mild correction and correspondence as discipline (versus corporal punishment)
rubrics_metrics.description: When pupils are discovered doing wrong, use mild admonition and moral appeal (example: a teacher writes a note pointing out the uneasiness of conscience and urging duty) rather than corporal punishment; such correspondence can prompt apology and reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare styles: one teacher strikes boys with a rule, eliciting tears and defiance; another writes an admonishing note which elicits a contrite written apology. The latter understanding of human nature is presented as preferable. Use private moral lectures, notes, or appeals to conscience to change behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly student reports by a Committee to monitor school order and propose remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Appoint a Committee (7–12 pupils) to prepare weekly written reports on the state of the school, noting specific faults (tardiness, whispering, disorder) and proposing remedies. The Committee may write in turn and may operate anonymously as desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports should mention concrete items, suggest remedies (but proposals may be rejected), note also good practices to encourage, and include suggested practical fixes (e.g., remove a bench obstructing a door). Rotate duties, accept suggestions from non-committee members in writing, and avoid running the measure continuously without change (it will otherwise become a mere form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Shopping exercise for arithmetic (practical, peer-calculated transactions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach making change by having pupils write items they'd like to buy (quantity and price, initially ≤10), have a neighbor compute the total, name a bill, and the neighbor compute change — the exercise passes down the line so each pupil practices both totaling and change-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with small numbers to avoid confusion; gradually allow higher numbers as skill improves. Watch for diversion into ludicrous examples (three meeting-houses at two cents) — permitting such frolics undermines attention and the main objective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discourage artifices in recitations; cultivate honest preparation and internal reward
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not tolerate prompting, peeping into books, or other artifice designed merely to 'appear' prepared. Emphasize that the object is faithful preparation and internal satisfaction; do not punish failures severely nor run a marking system ('no going up or down').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teacher models attitude: express that faithful preparation is the pupil's duty and reward is personal satisfaction; invite pupils to pledge honest conduct; avoid public punishment for failures; do not value mere appearance of knowledge over actual duty performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming and keeping definite resolutions (teach pupils specificity and experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach pupils to form definite, distinct resolutions — specify exactly what will be done, when to begin, and for how long (e.g., 'rise at the ringing of the sunrise bells' for one morning/one week), rather than vague, indefinite resolves like 'be more studious.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: deliberate before acting, then when action begins do not stop to reconsider. Make resolutions experiments of fixed duration to produce habit and avoid discouragement from vague aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic Exercise to build general information and oral expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign six or seven topics (e.g., 'Alabaster') to be researched and reported orally next day; at the exercise call all who have information to rise and let each state only one particular fact at a time so many pupils get to speak.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topics should begin with common objects and extend gradually. Benefits: induces reading from varied sources, develops discrimination in selecting important facts, and practices clear, confident verbal expression. Make the exercise voluntary but engaging to encourage wide participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize school singing with a chorister and Singing Committee
rubrics_metrics.description: If a sufficient number of singers exist, introduce singing as part of devotional exercises; obtain singing books, appoint a chorister to select tunes and lead, and assign one or two assistants to relieve initial embarrassment; form a Singing Committee to manage selections and scheduling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start gradually (some days may fail), gather hymn books, appoint leadership from willing pupils, and make singing regular; the committee can manage the exercise itself, turning it into a successful and interesting part of school life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'Tabu' labeling to protect delicate or consecrated objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Mark rare or fragile items (e.g., a delicate flower specimen) with a conspicuous 'TABU' label to indicate they are not to be touched, handled, or disturbed; pupils respect such marking more reliably than scolding or constant surveillance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ the word 'Tabu' (explained as 'consecrated, not to be touched') where apparatus or specimens would be injured by handling. This mild management technique protects property and teaches respect for shared items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental-analysis experiments to reveal differences in pupil rapidity and underlying causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use timed exercises (teacher gives an arithmetic example and times the shortest and longest students) to ascertain differences in rapidity among pupils; such experiments show variance not entirely due to skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe and analyze results to avoid simplistic assumptions about ability based solely on speed; use findings to inform instruction, pacing, and grouping. (Note: original text begins experiment and indicates difference is not altogether owing to skill.)
